status.reason: METHODS §6.4 'mixed' means inconsistent findings with no adequate explanation. What the claim asserts is that presentations show sympathomimetic and psychiatric features whose reported frequency varies several-fold between studies and settings, and that is reported consistently: independent series in different countries report tachycardia and hypertension (Fatovich et al., Perth; Lan et al., Taipei) and psychosis (Gray et al., Perth; Cloutier et al., Oregon; Pasic et al., Seattle; Szuster, Honolulu), and none reports their absence (Sibanda pp. 4–7, Table 1). The variation in frequency is part of the statement and is what different settings, case mixes and undefined denominators would produce; it belongs under GRADE inconsistency for the frequencies, not in a label that tells readers the studies disagree about whether these features occur. §6.4 allows counting primary studies listed in a review when the review reports their direction. The overlaps (Gray et al. in both reviews; the linked Perth and Oregon sets) are already stated. The reasoning's sentence 'Status mixed: the features recur across series, but their frequencies are inconsistent' would need rewording.

grade.proposed: very low (start low; risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1, indirectness −1; floor)
grade.reason: Start low (describes). Risk of bias −1 and indirectness −1 follow §6.3 for claims seen only through reviews (primary series not appraisable; second-hand; partly amphetamine or other stimulants). Inconsistency −1 is defensible for the frequency figures (hypertension 6.4% against 69%; psychosis 12% to 80%) and changes nothing at the floor; it concerns the frequencies, not the occurrence of the features, so it should not also be used to justify 'mixed'. Publication bias (case reports favour dramatic cases) and imprecision (no denominators) could also be argued, without effect.

plain.proposed: Meth poisoning can look like a body in overdrive: agitation, wide pupils, a racing heart, high blood pressure and fast breathing. Other signs include very high body temperature, chest pain, muscle breakdown, and heart, liver or kidney failure; seizures and coma are less common, and some people die. This picture comes from two reviews of hospital emergency studies and case reports; we have not yet checked the original studies, and some of them concern amphetamine rather than meth. How often each sign appears differs a lot between studies and settings: a racing heart was found in 42 of 100 patients in one study and in 85 of 100 in another, and psychosis in 12 to 80 of 100. Neither review says how many patients die. One review cites studies suggesting that many meth-related deaths come from accidents, suicide and homicide. Whether high body temperature predicts death has not been studied in the sources we have read.
plain.reason: Three small overstatements against the statement: 'Severe meth poisoning' adds a severity the sources do not restrict themselves to; 'Less often there is very high body temperature, chest pain ... or heart, liver or kidney failure' gives a frequency the statement does not (it calls these other features and says only coma and seizures are less frequent); and 'One review notes that many meth-related deaths come from accidents, suicide and homicide' drops the hedge (the review cites forensic studies suggesting this). The numbers in the plain text are right.

status.proposed: single-study (better: split into a US claim and an Australian claim, each single-study)
status.reason: The claim's own inconsistency note and reasoning say that the two surveys measure different quantities and that the gap 'is not heterogeneity in the GRADE sense'. I agree with that reading: one is DSM-III-R dependence among everyone who had ever used, at one interview; the other is DSM-IV abuse or dependence among people who may have used at least five times, at interview (45.7%) and as a 14-year projection (50.4%), and the Australian authors themselves say that counting abuse raises the estimates (Marel p. 139). Then there are no inconsistent findings on a common quantity and 'mixed' (§6.4) does not apply; each figure rests on one survey and neither replicates the other. 'Mixed' would tell readers that the surveys conflict, which the statement says cannot be judged. If the editors instead treat both as estimates of one base rate, 'mixed' needs inconsistency rated down as well (no change at the floor); the present combination (mixed with inconsistency 0) is internally inconsistent. Splitting the claim would make a single-study label literally true.

plain.proposed: An Australian survey from 2007 asked a different question. It estimated how many of the people who had used stimulants (it does not say which ones) would develop dependence or a related diagnosis called abuse within 14 years of first using them: about 50 in 100. About 46 in 100 had already had one of these diagnoses at some point by the time they were interviewed; the questions were asked only of people who had used at least five times.

The five-uses rule, which the statement gives, matters for the comparison with the US 'even once' denominator and is missing. Only the Australian sentence is changed; the rest of the plain text is faithful.

status.reason: Mixed is defensible on the review's evidence: the adjusted pool is 1.4 (0.8–2.4), the unadjusted pools have I² 95%, and the post hoc split gives violent behaviour 3.7 against violent offending 1.0 with I² 94% left unexplained within offending. The birth cohort agrees in direction with the review's adjusted estimate but does not resolve the behaviour-versus-offending inconsistency, and it shares two authors with the review (not data). Because inconsistency is not rated down, the reasoning should say what 'mixed' refers to (inconsistency across outcome types in the unadjusted data, while the adjusted estimates agree).

grade.proposed: very low (start low; risk of bias −1, imprecision −1; no dose-response upgrade)
grade.reason: Risk of bias −1 (review's violence studies among the lowest quality; cohort high on ROBINS-E) and imprecision −1 (review's adjusted interval includes 1; cohort lower limits 1.00–1.04) are right, and the floor is reached. Not upgrading for dose-response is right: the gradient (perpetration 1.13, 1.40, 4.84) comes from a model adjusted only for a reduced set of childhood and adolescent confounders; it relates the heaviest frequency in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35, so use and violence need not be in the same period or in that order (Foulds 2.7, p. 3); it rests on 51 people; the pairwise tests between frequency categories are not reported; and confounding by other drug use and drug-market involvement plausibly grows with frequency, away from the null. One correction to the reasoning: 'neither source can exclude no association after adjustment' is not accurate for the cohort, whose fully adjusted intervals exclude 1 for perpetration (1.01–2.54) and intimate-partner perpetration (1.04–2.30) and reach it for victimisation (1.00–2.47). Suggested: 'the review's adjusted interval includes no association, and the cohort's lower limits sit at 1.00–1.04 in one cohort at high risk of bias with same-period reporting'.
